extracted.intended_audience: journalists, editors and other reporters who cover traumatic events and survivors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for reporters and editors on how to research, interview, produce and publish stories about trauma survivors in ways that reduce harm, improve accuracy, and protect both sources and journalists. Includes interviewing techniques, consent practices, logistical planning, and self-care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand trauma's effects on the brain, memory and reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Trauma impacts the brain, including the memory and the ability to vocalize events as they happened. Trauma can significantly affect a person’s perception and judgment; when faced with traumatic situations, the brain can go into survival mode and people can suddenly feel and behave differently from their normal selves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize eyewitnesses to traumatic events may be unreliable and immediate accounts can differ from later, more accurate recollections. Be aware that survivors may literally be unable to tell coherent versions of events immediately after a tragedy. Consider timing of interviews and follow-ups — months later sources may recall differently. Use established definitions (e.g., SAMHSA) to frame what counts as trauma and its lasting effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Err on the side of overexplaining informed consent
rubrics_metrics.description: Informed consent in trauma-informed reporting means informing your sources about the nature of your story and having their consent to use their name and report on their experiences; journalists should err on the side of overexplaining.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume sources know terms like 'on the record' or 'on background' — explain clearly how they will or won't be identified. Offer options for anonymity or different levels of attribution. Make consent an ongoing conversation rather than a one-time checkbox.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer survivors review and ongoing consent for quotes and usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Give your sources the option to review their quotes or even to change their mind about being quoted before a story is published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing review can protect survivors from further harm and help ensure accuracy; consider allowing interviewed survivors to see the excerpts in which they're quoted, and make it clear how much control they have over final usage. Balance transparency with editorial constraints, and communicate timelines so survivors aren’t left in uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give power and agency to survivors during the interview and storytelling process
rubrics_metrics.description: Let your sources know that they have control of the situation — it’s acceptable to break some usual journalistic rules when interviewing trauma survivors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow sources to decline questions, see questions ahead of time if desired, choose what to answer, and indicate parts of their story they do not want published. Ask survivors what they want to achieve by telling their story. For audio/video/print productions, extend opportunities for survivors to include their voice in the process so they don’t feel talked about 'behind their back.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use trauma-specific interview etiquette (Dart Center guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow core interview behaviors: always treat victims with dignity and respect; clearly identify yourself; never say 'I understand' or 'I know how you feel'; don't overwhelm your source with the hardest questions first; if you receive a harsh reaction, leave contact information so survivors can follow up later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce yourself, make eye contact, explain why you want to talk, and take it slowly — do not 'stuff a microphone in someone’s face.' Prepare for a wide range of responses and respond with care, respect and kindness. These specific do/don’t examples are practical rules to follow during sensitive interviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask appropriate, open-ended questions and avoid distressing prompts
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid the overused and distressing question 'How do you feel?' and instead use alternatives such as 'How are you now?', 'How did you experience that?', or 'What do you think about …?'. Opt for open-ended questions and let subjects know they’re not required to answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use prompts like 'Where would you like to begin?' or 'Would you tell me what you are able to remember about your experience?' Avoid questioning why a source is emotional or minimizing their reaction. Frame questions to elicit information without re-traumatizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have a plan for interviews: pre-interview, during, and post-interview care
rubrics_metrics.description: Think about how you’re caring for survivors before, during and after the interview.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let survivors pick the interview location to help them feel safe. Tell them what questions you plan to ask and ask if there are questions to avoid. During the interview, monitor for signs of distress and offer breaks. At the end, thank your sources, explain how their interview will be used, and tell them when to expect the story or next contact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid surprise coverage — be transparent about production and publication
rubrics_metrics.description: If producing a podcast, video, or a printed story about a past crime or tragedy, make sure survivors are aware of the production and are extended the opportunity to include their voice and be part of the process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notify sources about planned projects that concern them; failing to do so can leave survivors feeling like the journalist is talking about them behind their back. Provide clear expectations about timelines and how their contributions will appear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize journalists' own mental well-being and recognize vicarious trauma
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists’ work covering traumatic events can affect their mental health; be aware of signs such as inability to concentrate, feeling on edge or numb, inability to feel compassion, sleep problems, anger, or increased substance use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow self-care practices: know your limits, take breaks, find a colleague who listens, maintain hobbies and relationships, and seek counseling if overwhelmed. Use organizational resources or training (e.g., Dart Center materials) to recognize and address secondary trauma; note prevalence estimates (4%–59% in some studies) to understand risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use established trauma-informed resources, style guides and training
rubrics_metrics.description: Rely on authoritative sources (for example, The Dart Center Style Guide for Trauma-Informed Journalism) to define trauma-related terminology and best practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult and link to comprehensive guides, training courses, and recommended readings (Dart Center guides, Transom pieces, Reynolds Institute resources, Poynter courses, books like The Body Keeps the Score) to inform reporting, editorial policies, and newsroom training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be willing to depart from standard newsroom rules when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Trauma-informed journalism may require 'forgetting all the rules that we usually abide by' and treating interview subjects differently than typical sources like officials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This can mean allowing questions to be previewed, permitting review of quotes, slowing interviews, and generally prioritizing survivor safety over standard expediency. Editors should support reporters in making these adaptations rather than penalizing deviations from standard procedure.
